# Hydra: picks the model best suited to each task, and can check the answer before you rely on it

> Hydra picks the model best suited to each task, and can check the answer before you rely on it. Technically it is a verified cascade gateway: an open source Go binary (`hyctl`) that sits in front of any model from any provider (hosted APIs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock or Mistral, local servers such as Ollama or llama.cpp, and CLI agents), ranks each one on its measured pass rate for the task type, and falls back to the next model when one fails. With a target set (`hyctl dispatch --confidence 0.95`, or the validator `hyctl edit` runs on the file it wrote), it checks the answer: verifiers and independent models add evidence until the posterior probability of being correct, P(correct), clears the target, and otherwise it asks the next-best model. A plain `hyctl dispatch` runs no verifier. Code is one task type among several, with its own verifiers (tests, compile, lint). No vendor is privileged.
>
> Today an unpinned request goes to the lowest-cost model that this machine has measured competent at the task type, with stronger models behind it as the fallback chain. Hydra counts a model as good enough at a task type only when it is still good enough after allowing for luck. A model that got 22 of 24 answers right may just have had a good run, and when several models are held to one bar, the one whose average clears it is often only the luckiest. So the bar is checked against the lowest rate the model's record supports at 95%, not against its average. 95% is the level `--confidence` uses by default. `--dry-run` prints both numbers, for example an average of 91 and at least 82 at 95%. A capability-first objective (`quality` / `balanced` / `cost`) is proposed in RFC 0001 (`docs/rfc/0001-verified-cascade-gateway.md`) and not yet shipped.

## Vocabulary

- **Model** or **source**: anything Hydra can ask, a hosted model, a local model, a CLI agent, or a verifier. Older docs and some identifiers call these "heads".
- **Task type**: the kind of work a request is, used to look up each model's measured pass rate. `hyctl dispatch --kind` names it from one fixed list: writing, summary, extraction, classification, translation, answer, analysis, agent, code. Some flags still call it `--domain`.
- **Routing level**: the fixed capability/price levels in `registry/routing.yaml` that `--enum` and `--tier` pin to (level 1 is the most capable, 10 the free local floor).
- **P(correct)** and **target**: the posterior probability that an answer is right, from per-source calibration, and the bar it must clear (`--confidence`).

## What It Does

- **Routing by task type and complexity**: every discovered model is placed on a routing level, from the most capable hosted models at level 1 down to free local models at level 10, and ranked within that on its measured pass rate for the task type
- **Interactive TUI cockpit**: `hyctl tui` opens an interactive cockpit whose chat **executes**: type a task and it runs, with a route line naming the routing level, model and strategy the router chose and why. The why names the kind of work from the fixed list (code for a file edit), or says it is not sure rather than guessing. Modes: Ask (the default: answers, never writes files), Edit, Plan, Auto (plan → edit → run your tests → fix → repeat, verified through `internal/oracle`), plus Architect/Careful/Unattended for more control. Six views: Chat · Agents · Models · Activity · Usage · Audit; `?` opens a shortcut glossary rendered from the keymap itself, and `ctrl+o` overrides where the next task runs. An answer is drawn as it arrives rather than all at once when the task finishes, and a model that gives up part-way through has its partial collapsed to one dim line naming the model and the reason, `e` expands it again, so a partial can never be mistaken for the answer. `hyctl tui --snapshot [--view 0..5]` renders one static frame for docs/previews
- **Desktop app**: a Wails v2 GUI in `desktop/` that opens on **Chat**: ask for work, and each reply says which model answered, at which routing level, and what it cost, with the run's timeline narrated live as it happens. The answer itself streams too: the reply grows as the model writes it, and when the router falls back the abandoned partial fades to a one-line summary naming the model and why it stopped, expandable to read what it had written, which is the same shape the CLI and the TUI show. The composer's model picker is grouped by **token pool**, so it shows when a choice spends a quota another model shares. Picking a model **pins** it: it is used or refused with a reason, never silently swapped for a different one, and when the router does fall back the reply names every model that could not answer and why. Beside the thread, a companion pane carries the active model, this run's confidence, per-model measured accuracy from the calibration record, and the files the run changed. Five more views sit behind the header's nav: **Models** (every model this machine can route to, grouped by the token pool it spends, each marked with whether anything can actually drive it right now and why not, plus the measured accuracy record, never a score without its outcome count), **Activity** (every request, grouped by who has to act: waiting on you, running now, something failed, done), **Usage** (spend, remaining context budget with the headroom in updates rather than a band name, and how many models a consensus check actually asked), **Audit** (what the agents did and whether the record can be trusted, OWASP LLM Top-10 coverage over the MCP audit log, the guardrail rules in force, and a safety verdict for every MCP server installed on this machine), and **Settings**, the only view that writes anything: the switches deciding where work may go (PII to a local model, refuse rather than send when nothing local is routable) and what is kept (prompt text, vectors, answers reused from a previous run), each stating what it costs rather than only what it is named, since every one is off by default for a reason. It overlays onto `~/.hydra/config.toml` rather than replacing it, so a setting it does not show cannot be lost by saving one it does, and a config that exists and does not parse is reported rather than rendered as defaults, because rendering defaults invites a save that discards what the file holds. Opening a request from Activity drills into **Session**: that run's timeline, a layered graph when it fanned out, and a Code tab whose diff marks what changed *within* a modified line and lets you accept or undo the change on disk. A ledger policy that answers `ask` parks the task and the question appears inline in the chat transcript, answerable there. Every release ships a build for macOS (universal), Windows x86-64/ARM64 and Linux x86-64/ARM64 on the releases page. The builds are not notarised yet, so the first launch on macOS needs System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway. The app runs Hydra in-process and needs no separate `hyctl` install: on first launch it asks for an API key (stored in the macOS Keychain or Windows Credential Manager, a 0600 file on Linux, any single-key provider Hydra supports) or a local model server, tests the key with one tiny request, then answers a sample question. Settings has the same **AI providers** section (add, test, remove; only a key's last four characters are ever shown) and the optional command-line tool. `hyctl` reads the same stored keys, with an exported variable taking precedence; a stored key never enters the process environment, so no subprocess (a CLI agent, a validator) inherits it. Can also be built from source with `cd desktop && wails build`
- **Per-run event log**: every dispatch writes `~/.hydra/logs/runs/<run_id>.jsonl`, model selection, swarm attempts, SPRT samples with their running confidence, A2A handoffs, and file edits, which is what the cockpit's Activity view and the desktop app reconstruct a run from. Every command that opens a run also records what the run is **for**, in one place, so a workflow, an edit and a fan-out are listed under their own task rather than under the routing key of whatever step happened to run first. `HYDRA_RUN_ID` groups invocations an external orchestrator spawns into one run
- **~1µs routing overhead**: the Go routing engine (policy eval + model selection + budget check) adds ~1,130 ns per dispatch, benchmarked on Apple M1 via `go test -bench=BenchmarkRoutingPath`
- **Swarm dispatch**: fan a single prompt to multiple models simultaneously, race (fastest), best (LLM-judged quality), or all (aggregate)
- **Confidence routing**: `hyctl dispatch --confidence 0.95` runs an SPRT (sequential probability ratio test) ensemble that samples models adaptively and stops once its estimate that the answer is correct clears a target (an estimate, not a guarantee; a mode with a stated error bound is planned in #1549), using per-source calibration (`hyctl trust calibration`) you build up from real outcomes, fewer model calls on easy tasks, more only where accuracy demands it. Calibration is a prerequisite: an uncalibrated source contributes no evidence, so a task type with none is refused with the command to record one rather than sampled at full cost for a coin-flip answer. The test is multi-hypothesis: every distinct answer stays under test for the whole run and each source is evidence about all of them, so nothing is discarded when the leading answer changes, and a run where every model gives a different answer reports low confidence rather than picking one. Calibration is trained from whole ensemble runs, not just accepted answers (`hyctl trust outcome <task_hash> --outcome correct|incorrect`), because a source that disagreed with an answer that turned out wrong is the only observation that measures specificity; `hyctl trust calibration` prints a `neg` count per source and marks every cell whose verdicts all point one way. Such a cell contributes **0 nats**, whatever its apparent accuracy: a source that has only ever answered one way has not discriminated between anything, and the Laplace prior that is meant to leave it uninformative instead deformed it, since with no negative verdict the specificity cell keeps its bare prior while false positives accumulate, so `ln(se/(1-sp))` crossed zero at about seven failures and went negative past it. A model whose own edits had failed then counted as evidence *against* any answer it agreed with, and with two such models proposing different answers both candidates landed below the 50% prior, which is why ensemble runs reported less than a coin flip. The rates still print, because they are what the counts say, but they describe the prior rather than the source until evidence arrives in both directions. Calibration is keyed per source and task type, and a run naming a file (`--file`) resolves the same task type that `hyctl edit` and `hyctl review` record outcomes under, so evidence built up while working on a file is the evidence a later confidence run reads. Every run prints its own task hash and the `hyctl trust explain` command for it, so the per-source evidence ledger, the per-hypothesis log-odds, and whether the run stopped because it reached its target or because the budget ran out, are one copy-paste away. An ensemble run also records the **span** it ran under, which is the identifier a verdict arrives on, so `hyctl oracle verify --span <id>` replays that run's ledger into calibration by itself: the oracle ran a real command, so the verdict comes from outside the run rather than from its own answer, and the models that dissented are trained along with the ones that agreed. Before that the two sides of the loop had no join key and a human had to carry a task hash from one command to another, which across seventeen real ensemble runs on a working machine nobody ever did. One ledger is replayed once, whether it is reached through the span or through `hyctl trust outcome <task_hash>`, because replaying it twice would count every vote twice
- **The loop closes where the answer is applied**: `hyctl edit` writes the change to disk and then runs the language validator against that file, so its pass or fail is about the content the model actually produced. That verdict trains the per-source calibration and fills the oracle-verified corpus, rejections included. It deliberately does not happen on a plain dispatch: a dispatch writes nothing, so a verifier would judge the repository as it already was, and recording that would be confident false evidence about every model that answered
- **Confidence you can audit**: `hyctl trust reliability` asks whether the stated number is honest, when Hydra says 90% is it right 90% of the time, by pairing each confidence-routed run with the verdict later recorded against it (`hyctl trace score`, or an oracle). It reports a Brier score decomposed as reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty, so a router that merely states the base rate cannot look well calibrated, plus ECE and a reliability diagram, and it refuses to report at all below twenty judged runs rather than drawing a diagram from noise `--source <head>` runs the same audit on each decision source, per task type and side by side, so you can see which one is honest on your own work.
- **Checks that fail together**: every verdict on an answer (tests, lint, a grounding check, a model vote, a person's review) goes into one log beside the eval corpus. `hyctl trust joint` reports, per kind of work, how often each check and each pair of checks passed an answer that later turned out wrong, with a one-sided 95% upper bound and the rate the pair would have if the two failed independently. Each check's rate is also watched for a change (a test suite that stops covering a path, a judge model swapped), and a changed check shows when and its rate and bound since (`changed`, `since` in `--json`). Below 20 shared wrong answers it prints no rate
- **Blast-radius aware**: `hyctl dispatch --file X` and `hyctl graph blast X` read a code dependency graph (`graph.json`) so an edit to a widely-depended-on file demands higher confidence than a leaf, the defect-cost model holds expected leaked-defect cost roughly constant
- **Token budget enforcement**: pressure modes (Normal → Emergency) plus a rate-aware first-passage governor auto-downgrade routing levels as the orchestrator's context window fills
- **Cost analytics**: `hyctl stats` shows spend broken down by model, routing level, and day
- **Traces that answer counterfactuals**: every dispatch row records the probability the router chose its first pick (`act_prob`, naming that pick in `first_head` and how far the fallback chain went in `fallback_step`) and the probability the row was kept (`keep_prob`). Without them a sampled log cannot be corrected back to the population. In simulation, averaging a non-uniformly sampled log inverted the true ranking of two models, which would then change routing. Storage is bounded by keeping statistics rather than text: mergeable quantile sketches for latency, oracle verdicts as a permanent labelled corpus, and old run logs sealed into compressed monthly segments
- **Prompt caching**: on by default for every request, any kind of work. `prompt_cache: true` in `registry/policy.yaml` asks providers that cache only when asked (Anthropic) to cache the system prompt and tool list; OpenAI, Gemini and DeepSeek cache on their own. Cache reads are logged and priced at the model's cache rate. A policy rule with `prompt_cache: false` turns it off for the work it matches
- **Routing rules in config, not in code**: `registry/signals.yaml` turns a dispatch into named, typed facts (each PII detector separately, including `pii.phone_number.matched` and `pii.iban.matched`, a prompt-injection marker, the target file's blast radius, keyword sets you declare, whether calibration has evidence for this task type, the prompt's dominant Unicode script and, where the script settles it, its language, the prompt's shape as counts of questions, list items, code fences and ordered steps, the conversation's turn count and whether it is already in a tool loop, and the estimated prompt tokens) and combines them with priority-ordered rules into an action: pin a routing level or enum, force local-only, raise the confidence bar, or refuse the dispatch. Evaluated once per dispatch and reused across every fallback candidate, so a rule cannot answer differently for two attempts at one task. The expression language is closed (`&& || ! ( ) == != < <= > >=`) and parses to a typed tree at load, so a rule naming a signal that does not exist, or comparing a number to a string, fails at load with the rule named rather than silently never matching. It ships **empty**, so routing is unchanged until you write a rule; `hyctl dispatch --dry-run` names the rule that fired and the signals it read, and `hyctl security` reports any rule that can never fire. A signal nothing measured is **absent**, and a comparison against an absent signal never matches whatever the operator, so `graph.blast_radius < 5` does not fire on a dispatch that read no blast radius: an absent number used to compare as zero, which made every low-bound rule fire on evidence nobody had. `language.code` is reported only where the script decides the language (kana means Japanese, hangul Korean, Han alone Chinese) and is **absent** for Latin script, because separating English from French needs a model or an unmeasured threshold and a guessed default would route on a coin flip. `conversation.turns` is likewise absent rather than zero on a single-shot dispatch, since that is not a conversation of length zero, while `structure.questions` is always present because a count of zero questions is a reading. Three of the signals come from the verified corpus, `corpus.known`, `corpus.pass_rate` and `corpus.support`, so a rule can route on what actually passed for work like this rather than on the routing key the caller guessed. Those three are derived only when a rule names one, because each costs an embedding call and a pass over the corpus, and whether the estimate is worth routing on at all is what `hyctl eval classify` reports. What the PII detectors actually catch is measured rather than claimed: against the presidio-research synthetic set some detector fires on 18.7% of the 1,387 texts carrying PII, 100% of emails, SSNs and IBANs, 93% of cards and IP addresses, 69% of phone numbers, and nothing at all for names, street addresses and organisations, which is 1,509 spans with no pattern to write and the honest reason a trained NER model is a separate piece of work. A phone number is recognised by a country code, a parenthesised area code, the 3-3-4 grouping or a trunk zero, never by a bare run of digits, and both detectors are guarded by a vendored sample so a recall regression is a red build rather than a number in a pull request.
- **An answer cache that refuses**: `hyctl trace cache` reports the opt-in store of previous answers, off unless chosen at `hyctl init`. A cache is the one part of a router that fails by returning a confident answer to a question nobody asked, so an exact match on the normalized prompt is the only thing served outright; anything else must ask exactly the same thing: the same content words, in the same order, function words aside, and then clear a cosine threshold (0.95 by default) where an embedding model exists. The content gate is what finds the candidate, so the cache works on a machine with no embedding model at all rather than degrading to an exact hash map, and the dense half is an upgrade on that candidate rather than a precondition for having one: over the same 79,800 pairs the content gate alone refuses every one, while cosine alone still serves 79 at 0.85. On a machine with no embedder a restatement is served exactly when it keeps every content word in the same order, which is all 400 of the corpus for punctuation, whitespace and filler words, and 369 of 400 when the prompt is uppercased, because uppercasing a camelCase identifier really does change the words. Order is load-bearing rather than incidental, because it is what carries the direction of an operation and the dense half reads a question and its reverse as more alike than an average restatement: six order-swapped pairs measure 0.9736 to 0.9913 cosine, above the threshold, so asking for a higher similarity makes that case worse rather than better. Measured on 400 real commit subjects, 79,800 distinct pairs every one of which must be refused: cosine alone would serve 79 of them at 0.85 and 1 at 0.95, and the content gate takes every threshold to zero, while still serving 100% of restatements that differ only in whitespace or punctuation and 95% that add filler words. The question is more than the prompt: the system prompt that framed it and the output cap it was produced under are both in the key, so `--system "the secret code is ALPHA"` and `--system "…BRAVO"` are two questions rather than one, and the entry records which instructions produced it so the store can be audited. An answer the head reported as capped is not stored at all, because a fragment replayed later reads as a whole answer and is reported as having finished normally. An answer from a weaker tier is never served to a stronger request, or escalating with `--tier <lower-number>` after a bad answer would hand back the answer being escalated away from; serving down is still allowed, since a stronger head's answer is at least as good. A prompt carrying personal data or an injection marker is never served or stored, a pinned model is never answered from another model's work, and a confidence-routed run cannot reach the cache at all because the ensemble samples models directly. A hit writes no cost row: it has no model and so no routing propensity, and a row carrying an invented one would corrupt every counterfactual computed afterwards
- **Off-policy evaluation**: `hyctl trace evaluate --policy cheaper` estimates what a routing policy you never ran would have cost, with a confidence interval, and refuses where the log cannot answer. It weights each row by the probability of the router's first pick and asks the other policy about that pick, not about a fallback that answered after it, and it counts older rows that do not record the first pick. `--policy constraint` asks the same question of the cheapest-measured-competent router itself, reading each row's recorded task type and comparing the model that ran against the model that policy would choose for it today. `hyctl trace export --otlp` ships the same dispatches to any OpenTelemetry collector (Langfuse, Grafana, Jaeger) without giving up Hydra's own schema
- **Dynamic pricing**: live rates from OpenRouter API with 24h cache and static YAML offline fallback
- **Any API key works**: set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `GROQ_API_KEY`, `MISTRAL_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY` (or Bedrock/Azure/Cohere/Replicate/Together/Fireworks/Perplexity credentials; the Bedrock model speaks the model-agnostic Converse API, so any Bedrock model id routes, and it resolves AWS credentials the way every other AWS tool does, the environment first and then `AWS_PROFILE` or `default` out of `~/.aws/credentials` and `~/.aws/config`, so a machine configured the way the AWS CLI expects shows the model rather than reporting no Bedrock at all; a profile declaring role_arn, sso_session or credential_process is refused whatever static keys sit beside it in that profile, though credentials exported in the environment are untouched, since the environment comes first in the AWS chain and no other AWS tool would read the profile at all, since those keys obtain the identity rather than being it and signing with them would act as the wrong principal; Hydra performs no token exchange, so the model reads as unroutable and says which of the credential, the region or the model is the missing one) and the provider becomes a routable model automatically, no config file to touch. `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` and `CO_API_URL` (the variables the official SDKs read, plus `GEMINI_BASE_URL` and `COHERE_BASE_URL` as the spellings several tools use) point those models at a gateway instead, and the streamed and buffered paths resolve the host together so neither can quietly keep calling the provider directly
- **Routing within OpenRouter**: a key alone gives one routing choice: a single model. Hydra already prices and scores OpenRouter's whole catalogue, so `[openrouter] models = [...]` in `~/.hydra/config.toml` turns each named model into its own routing choice the router picks between on cost and capability, replacing the single key-derived model rather than sitting beside it (two models on one account split its spend). Admission is explicit because enumerating hundreds of models would bury `probe` and `status`, and top-N or usage-based rules are just ways of computing the same list. `probe` says how much of the catalogue is enabled ("2 of 423"); a name the catalogue does not hold is shown as not routable with the reason rather than dropped, and an unfetched catalogue refuses nothing, since it is no evidence either way. Scores come from the same heuristic `hyctl models sync` records, so ranking does not depend on having run one, and `hyctl models add` still overrides it
- **Egress gate**: a file is classified by **where it is**, not by what is inside it, so a whole category is closed whether or not its contents match a detector. Env files, private keys, cloud and cluster credentials, tfstate, SSH and package-manager config and `~/.hydra` itself are refused to any model that leaves the machine; work naming one is rerouted to a local model and the user is told, never silently swapped. With no local model routable the default refuses rather than falling back to the network (`[egress] strict`, default true, and a config with no `[egress]` section reads as strict). Rules live in `registry/sensitivity.yaml`, embedded and overridable without a rebuild, with an `allow` list so a committed `.env.example` is not treated as a secret. The gate fails closed in both directions that matter: an error denies, and a payload declaring no provenance is refused, so a code path that forgets the gate breaks loudly rather than leaking quietly. The boundary is stated rather than implied: CLI agents read files on their own, so Hydra guarantees what it sends, not what a subprocess agent independently reads, and the guarantee is total only on a local model
- **Least-privilege agents**: an agent subprocess gets the base environment (PATH, HOME, locale, proxy), its own provider's credential and its own tool configuration, and nothing else. Every agent subprocess previously inherited the full environment, so an agy subprocess held `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, every other provider's key and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`. `HYDRA_HEAD_ENV=VAR1,VAR2` restores a variable the allowlist does not know a tool needs, since no allowlist over third-party CLI agents can stay complete. Model subprocesses are bounded so a grandchild holding the pipe open cannot hang a call on a process that already exited; process-group isolation is deliberately not used, because Hydra installs no SIGINT handler, so it would orphan a model on Ctrl+C to prevent a rarer orphan on timeout. Hydra never starts a model server: a local model exists only while one is already answering, so nothing it spawns can read `$OLLAMA_HOST` and bind wide. Local model weights are fingerprinted by digest alongside agent binaries, so a swapped model behind a familiar name is detected the way a replaced agent binary is, which matters because Ollama pulls unsigned weights from a public registry. Validators, oracles, `--check cmd:` and `hyverify` get the base environment plus toolchain paths (GOPATH, GOCACHE, GOFLAGS, NODE_PATH, npm_config_cache and similar) and no credential; `validator_env:` in `workspace.yaml` (or `hyverify --env`) adds a variable a check needs, and a credential-like name is refused and listed by `hyctl security`. They still run with the user's file and network access: containment there needs a platform sandbox and is tracked separately. Model-written code that must run offline gets no network at all, loopback included: a network namespace on Linux, `sandbox-exec` with a deny-network profile on macOS. Where neither can be set up (Windows, Linux without user namespaces, Ubuntu 24.04's default AppArmor rule) it is not run and reads as "not checked: no network isolation", never a pass; `hyctl security --why` says which applies. It can still read and write the user's files, and on Linux a Unix socket with a path stays reachable
- **A2A handoff**: structured JSON context (with vector clocks for causal ordering) passed between agents across tasks

## CLI Commands

- `hyctl dispatch`: send a request to a model measured capable at its task type, with automatic fallback (`--enum`/`--tier`, `--kind`, `--swarm`, `--confidence`, `--file`, `--local`, `--dry-run`, `--a2a`, `--no-stream`, `--check`, `--source-only`). `--kind summary` ranks models on their record for that kind of work and logs the request under `summary.general`; `--kind extraction.invoices` names an area too. An unknown kind fails before anything routes, and `--kind` with `--domain` is refused. `--check ground` checks the answer against the context the prompt fenced: every number, date, name and identifier in it, and every phrase of three or more words it puts in double quotes, has to appear in the prompt, and any that do not are listed. The verdict is scored on the span that answered, so `hyctl trace view` shows it. A check that really fails reruns the request once on a model measured stronger at that kind of work, sent the rejected answer and the error, within the same `--max-cost`, even past a pinned `--tier` or `--enum`; a check that could not run never reruns, and both answers are filed under the model that wrote them. `--max-escalations` sets how many reruns (default from `max_retries` and `escalate_on_fail` in `policy.yaml`, `0` turns it off). A prompt with no fenced context, or an answer with nothing checkable in it, prints "not checked", never a pass. `--check links` fetches each URL in the answer, at most 20, with a short timeout, a 2 MB cap and three redirects: a link that does not resolve fails, and so does a quote of three or more words, in the same sentence as the link, that none of that sentence's pages holds once tags are stripped and case and spacing folded. It is off unless named. Each fetch is a network action, so the MCP ledger is asked first and records it, and only the URL leaves the machine, never the answer or the prompt. An answer with no links, a fetch the ledger denies, or no network at all prints "not checked", never a pass. `--check citations` looks up each DOI at doi.org (CSL JSON by content negotiation) and each arXiv id (`arXiv:1706.03762`, `arxiv.org/abs/...`) at the arXiv API, all arXiv ids in one request: an id that does not exist fails with the id named, and so does a quoted title in its sentence that differs from the record once case and punctuation are folded. It is gated by the ledger like `--check links`, only the id leaves the machine, and each lookup is cached for a day under `~/.hydra/cache/citations`, so a rerun asks nothing. A service that does not answer is "not checked". An answer that failed a check, or whose check could not run, ends with one line, "not verified: <check>: <reason>". `--require-pass` makes that the exit code, the same ones `hyctl oracle ground` uses: 0 when every check passed, 1 when one failed, 2 when none failed but one could not run, so a script or CI job can gate on it. It needs a `--check` and is refused with `--dry-run`. `--check match:labels=<file>` passes an answer that is one of the labels in the file (one per line), and `--check match:pattern=<re>` one the whole of which matches the pattern, so a classification can be checked. `--check sum:total=items[].amount` passes an answer whose line amounts add up to its total, and `--check sum:total=subtotal,tax` one whose named fields do, with no model call: amounts may carry thousands commas and a leading currency symbol or code, they have to match within half of the total's last written digit, and a fail shows both numbers, so an invoice or receipt total the model made up is caught. A missing path or a value that is not a number fails and is named. `--check gen` on an extraction adds the same check, as `gen:sum-<total>`, for each total the field list writer says should add up, kept only when the total and its parts are fields it listed. `--check cmd:<command>` runs any command given the answer as `{answer}` or as a file at `{file}`, and exit 0 passes, so an extraction can be checked by a schema tool: `hyctl dispatch --check 'cmd:check-jsonschema --schemafile invoice.json {file}' "pull the invoice number and total from this email as JSON"`. The command is split on spaces, and one with neither placeholder is refused before anything routes, since it could not see the answer. Each check is calibrated under its own source, `verifier:match:<labels file or pattern>` or `verifier:<command>`. `--check gen` writes checks for the request's kind of work (`--kind` is required; without it the line says "not checked: no kind of work") with a model of another family where one exists, runs them on the answer, prints one line per check and a label (all passed, some failed, not checked), and logs each verdict as `gen:<check>`. A classification gets its label set, an extraction its fields (every field gets a verdict, and each one that is not ok prints on its own line: missing, wrong_type, not_in_source, absent for an optional field not given, or unverified when the prompt fenced no source to check a copied value against, then how many fields were ok), an answer, summary or analysis a grounding and a judge check per sentence, writing a yes/no rubric, and code, with `gen:tests=<file>` naming the file the answer replaces, Go tests another model writes, run on a copy of the module before and after the change with the network off; a test that fails both times is dropped as suspect, and another language, no file or no network isolation is not checked. `--schema invoice.schema.json` gives the fields check its field list from a JSON Schema instead of asking a model: the top-level `properties` with their `type` (string, number or integer, boolean, array) and `required`, and an object one level down as dotted names such as `address.city`. It implies `--check gen:fields` (kind `extraction` unless `--kind` says otherwise) and makes no extra model call. Strings and numbers have to appear in the prompt's fenced source when it has one. Deeper nesting is refused before anything routes, and keywords it does not read, such as `minLength` or `$ref`, are named in one warning line. A schema with more fields than `--max-fields` (default 30) is asked for in chunks, in schema order with an object's fields kept together, every chunk on the head that answered the first and with the same fenced source, so a provider cache can reuse it. The objects are merged, a key two chunks both give is reported and not overwritten, the cost is the sum of the chunks, and the checks run once on the merged object. `--check gen:<check>` runs one, e.g. `gen:roundtrip`, which re-extracts the fields with the other model and is never run by plain `gen` because it costs a call. Run beside `gen:fields`, each field prints once: `in_source_and_agreed`, `in_source`, `agreed`, or what failed, and `differs` shows both values. Generated checks only report: they never rerun the request. `--source-only` is for support replies and other answers that must stay inside given documents: it refuses a prompt with no fenced source, tells the model to answer only from it, and checks every sentence of the reply against it with the grounding and judge checks above, for any `--kind`, `writing.support` included. A failed reply reruns once on a stronger model. If no reply passes, hyctl prints "the documents given do not cover this" and the sentences that failed, never the reply, and exits 1; when the reply could not be checked at all it exits 2. `--max-usd` caps what the answer and its generated checks spend; past it, the rest print "not checked: budget". `--check` runs on a single dispatch, not with `--swarm` or a confidence run. On a terminal the answer is drawn as it arrives, with a spinner covering the wait before the first token and the token counts, elapsed time and measured TTFT as a footer once the call returns. The OpenAI-compatible shape (local servers such as Ollama and LM Studio included), Azure, Anthropic, Gemini, Cohere, Bedrock and CLI agents stream token by token, every HTTP dialect Hydra speaks except Replicate, whose prediction API polls rather than streams. agy streams too, with its leading output held back until the sign-in check has run: that check reads stderr, which is unreadable until the process exits, so forwarding as it arrives would render an interactive auth prompt as the model's answer. A run that needs a sign-in therefore emits nothing at all, and the time to first token is when output arrived rather than when the hold-back released it. A model that cannot stream delivers its whole output as a single update rather than rendering differently. Piped output is never streamed and is byte-identical to before, so scripts are unaffected; `--no-stream` asks for the same buffered rendering on a terminal. A fan-out has no single stream to show, so `--swarm` and `--confidence` draw a live panel instead: every model that was selected, with its state, elapsed time, tokens and the cost as it accrues, and for a confidence run the running log-odds against the threshold it has to cross, so an ensemble that stops after two models says why it stopped rather than only that it did. The panel is erased when the run ends and the result printed after it is unchanged. When a model fails part-way through, its partial output is collapsed off the screen and replaced by one line naming the model and the reason, since a partial that stays on screen reads as part of the answer. `--tier` takes a number 1-10 or a name, and a name is the lowercase of a routing enum, so `--tier simple`, `--enum SIMPLE` and `--tier 8` are one instruction. Both flags read `registry/routing.yaml`, so retuning a routing level there moves them together, and both reach a fan-out: `--enum` used to be read only by the single-dispatch path, so `--swarm` and `--confidence` selected the strongest models by capability whatever routing key was asked for. `--tier local` is the one alias, a legacy name for `grunt`, the free local floor. With neither flag given, the choice is a **constraint rather than a ladder**: the cheapest model this machine has measured competent at the task's task type runs the task, and the stronger models become the fallback chain behind it. A routing level number is a price, which really is one-dimensional, and was doing double duty as a competence gate, which is not: a model strong enough for hard Go is not thereby strong enough for hard SQL. Competence has to have been measured *in this task type*, at least twenty judged answers, and it is compared against the confidence the defect model already demands of an ensemble, so nothing new is invented to make the comparison and a machine with no history routes exactly as it always did. Once two models both clear the bar the cheaper one wins outright, since picking the better of two competent models is the ladder again with more steps. A named routing level or enum is a user instruction and is obeyed as one, the constraint decides only where nothing was pinned. `--dry-run` prints the bar, what each model was measured at and on how much evidence, what a call to it costs, and whether it cleared. When the model that answered, or one passed over on its record, got worse or recovered at this kind of work in the last 14 days, one dim line under the route line says so ("summary record for <model> changed on 12 Nov"); nothing is printed otherwise
- `hyctl probe`: scan the machine for every available model (CLI agents, API keys, local servers). A running **LiteLLM** proxy is discovered too, one entry per model it fronts rather than one entry for the proxy, read from `/model/info` at `LITELLM_PROXY_URL` with `LITELLM_PROXY_API_KEY`, the variables LiteLLM's own client reads. Whether such a model counts as local is decided **per model from the upstream the proxy reports**, never from its address: a proxy on localhost forwarding to OpenAI is the normal deployment, and treating that as local would price a paid model at the free routing level and hand the local-only PII policy a model that leaves the machine. An upstream the proxy does not report is treated as not local, since that error is merely expensive. A proxy that is running but whose model list cannot be read is listed as discovered and not routable, naming the key to set, rather than not appearing at all. A running **llama.cpp** server is discovered as well, one entry per model it has loaded, read from `/v1/models` at the address `LLAMA_ARG_HOST`/`LLAMA_ARG_PORT` name, with `LLAMA_API_KEY` where the server was started with one. It is **identified rather than assumed from its port**: 8080 is the most common port on a developer's machine, so the probe requires llama.cpp's own `build_info` on `/props` before it reports anything, and an unrelated service there yields no models. The window it reports is the one it actually allocated, so it replaces the local default rather than capping it: a server started with a large `-c` used to be budgeted at 4096 regardless. For a local model it reports the quantization the server actually loaded (`Q4_K_M`, `Q8_0`, `F16`) and the parameter count, read from what the server reports rather than guessed: the same model id at two quants differs in accuracy, VRAM and tokens/sec, so routing them as one model hides the tradeoff. A server that reports no quantization gets no column and no invented value. The score a model is listed under is the one it was **ranked** on: the catalogue's number updated by this machine's own verified history, so a model that keeps being wrong sinks below one the catalogue rates higher. Where that happened the table shows what it was adjusted from and on how many judged answers, and below twenty of those nothing moves at all, so a fresh install ranks exactly as it always did. There is no per-quantization penalty table: a 2-bit model is outranked once it has been measured, never because a hardcoded number said it should be. A dispatch that knows its task type (`--domain`, or derived from `--file`) goes further and ranks on what each model got right *at that kind of work*, so a model strong at Go and weak at SQL stops being routed both as though it were the same model. Evidence from other task types still counts, since a model thin in one task type should borrow from its own record rather than be judged on three runs, but only up to a bound: without one, a model measured everywhere except here outranked a model measured here, and the task type made no difference at all. `--dry-run` names the model, what it was ranked on, and how much of that evidence came from this task type rather than another. `--json` additionally carries the architectural context ceiling, which caps the window the budget governor holds that model to; it is deliberately not the effective window, since a 40960-token model still runs at its server's default
- `hyctl status`: session state, the rate-aware `claude_pct` budget governor, and the models that can actually run right now, grouped by the routing level they would route at, with the `--tier`/`--enum` words that reach each routing level on the same row. A name whose routing level nothing currently sits at is reported as such rather than left off, since it still routes by degrading to the cheapest model available
- `hyctl tui`: interactive cockpit whose chat executes (Ask by default, then Edit/Plan/Auto, plus Architect/Careful/Unattended; an empty chat offers four mixed starter tasks, 1-4 fills one in), plus five more views over the same data: Agents, Models, Activity, Usage, Audit. Usage shows cost per passed answer over 30 days with its pass rate and 95% interval, beside the best single model on your own record for the same kind of work, and shows no figure until 30 answers have been checked. The Models view says, per kind of work, when a model got worse (with its record since) or came back to normal, and an empty chat names up to three models that did either in the last 7 days
- `hyctl cost`: spend report (estimated vs actual) from the dispatch cost log. `est_cost_usd` prices cache reads and writes at the model's cache rates where it lists them, and at the input rate where it does not; a cache column (tokens read, share of input) appears once any row has them
- `hyctl stats`: session cost rollup by model, routing level, and day. `--latency` reports p50/p90/p99 per model from mergeable relative-error sketches held in per-day rollups, so a percentile is answered without rescanning the whole cost log and two machines' stats can be combined without shipping their traces
- `hyctl pricing`: live pricing DB (`list`, `refresh`)
- `hyctl trust`: per-source calibration and verification (`calibration`, `record`, `defect`, `stats`, `explain`). `calibration` (and `--json`) also shows, per source and kind of work, when a drop in how often it is right was found (`changed`), when it got back to its old rate after that (`recovered`), and its record since (`since_correct`/`since_total`). A source nobody is calling relaxes back toward a fresh record while others in the same kind of work are judged, so a fixed model is not held to its old misses for ever. Routing ranks each model on its record since the last change in that kind of work, so one that got worse loses its place within tens of answers. Measured in simulation: a drop from 90% to 74% right is found after a median 89 answers, smaller drops or lower base rates usually not within 200, at about 0.03 false alarms a month at 1,000 answers a month
- `hyctl graph`: code dependency graph. `blast` gives blast radius + percolation-κ, `parallel` the optimal agent count
- `hyctl context`: context signal density / entropy governor (`entropy`)
- `hyctl mcp`: local MCP accountability ledger (`check`, `record`, `verify`, `log`, `report`, `verify-chain`). Access checks can be classification-aware (PII/prompt-injection-marker auto-detected from content) and bind a SHA256 hash of the invocation parameters, so `verify` can later prove the executed parameters match the ones that were approved. Every event is hash-chained and anchored: `verify-chain` detects post-hoc edits, deletions from the middle, **and deletion from the end** (a truncated tail leaves every surviving link valid, so it is caught by comparing the log against the chain anchor rather than by walking it) and can carry an optional MITRE ATLAS/OWASP LLM Top-10 `Framework` tag. `check` exits 0 on allow, 3 on deny and **4 on ask**, since ask withholds permission pending a human and exiting 0 made it indistinguishable from approval to the script the exit code exists for. Ask is counted and filterable everywhere deny is: `report` breaks it out, `log --denied` lists withheld accesses (deny and ask), and `security --why` reports it as awaiting approval. `log` shows the classification an event was evaluated under, and a rule's classification scope is rendered in the policy audit and in the recorded reason, so a rule that denies only PII-classified egress no longer reads as a universal deny. `verify` prints the anchor caveat beside MATCH when the chain anchor is missing or stale, since deletion from the end cannot be ruled out there and a bare MATCH read as a verification against a provably complete log
- `hyctl mcp registry`: safety score for the MCP servers actually installed on your machine. `sync` (pull the official MCP registry), `scan` (find installed servers across Claude Code/Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, identity only, never reads env/secret values), `audit` (resolve + score + advance lifecycle state), `export` (static `index.html`/`index.json` of audited servers, no hosting), `backtest` (validate the scoring pipeline against known real incidents, `postmark-mcp`'s rug-pull, CVE-2025-6514), `clear` (recover a server quarantined in error). Scoring follows the CSA MCP Selection Scorecard's four categories. Every version bump drops a server's status back to provisional until it re-earns it, the direct fix for a server that ships clean for months, then turns malicious in a later version. So does a rewritten tool: each tool's name, description and input schema is hashed, and `audit` prints the before and after. Descriptions are checked for text aimed at the model (directions about other tools, file-read or send-data requests, hidden characters, over-long padding), each a finding with its exact span that never quarantines on its own. Both read a saved `tools/list` result at `$HYDRA_HOME/mcp_tools/<server>.json`; `audit` never starts a server, and reports "not checked" without one. Auto-classifies ledger events (`mcp-unverified`/`mcp-flagged`/`mcp-quarantined`) so `hyctl mcp check` can gate on it automatically. Also flags `mcp-behavior-change`: a server whose local ledger history has only ever shown one action type (e.g. read) performing another (e.g. network) for the first time, catchable from this machine's own history alone, no registry data or CVE required. A server's first-ever call is never flagged `audit` also fingerprints each tool's name, description and input schema from a saved `tools/list` result at `~/.hydra/mcp_tools/<server>.json`: a description rewritten after approval drops the server back to provisional, and text in a description aimed at the model rather than the user is reported with its exact span. A server with no saved list says its tools were not checked.
- `hyctl egress receipt [run-id]`: per model a run asked (default the last run): provider, local or remote, sensitivity, and how many values of each kind it saw as placeholders and got back restored, with whether the ledger hash chain verifies. `--json`. Counts only, never a value or a hash of one.
- `hyctl security`: answers one question by default: what did the agents on this machine actually do, and can the record be trusted. Prints a **verdict** (act now / attention / ok) with the single condition that produced it, a state machine over facts, never a blended score, the **correlated incident** behind it (risky ledger events grouped per actor into an attack sequence: injection → recon → escalation → audit-tampering, rated by OWASP Risk Rating likelihood × impact) and the **evidence state** (how many events, how many hash-chained, and whether the chain is intact, broken, truncated or unanchored). Roughly a dozen lines, no tables. `--why` opens the full programme underneath it: a **risk register** where every finding is one governed object (stable ID, severity, SLA clock with breach detection, per-defect cost from the router's own defect model, and a curated crosswalk to OWASP LLM / NIST AI RMF / ISO 42001 / MITRE ATLAS / SOC 2), an OWASP LLM Top-10 coverage score (percentage of applicable categories with a live, evidence-backed mechanism, hard-overridden to "INTEGRITY COMPROMISED" if the ledger chain is tampered with, and withheld entirely while the access policy is fail-open, since a coverage number describes mechanisms that are not actually in force; a category whose mechanism is detective rather than preventive reads `partial` and does not count as covered), a **policy audit** (per-rule hit counts, rules that never matched, rules provably unreachable, and whether the default is fail-open), **sensitive-data exposure** (every PII detection named by type and resolved against the discovered models to say whether it stayed local or reached a model that leaves the machine, with unidentified models reported separately rather than counted as confirmed leaks), a **threat breakdown**, a **control-effectiveness audit** (a control that is configured but never applied is reported as inert rather than reading as protection, and a `registry/policy.yaml` condition naming no real task field is named with its rule, since such a rule can never fire and an operator reading the file cannot otherwise tell that from one that has simply not come up), **confidence evidence quality**, **configuration stability**, **agent-binary integrity** (change detection, not provenance), **edit blast radius** (a file the graph does not index is reported as unknown, never as low-risk), least-privilege review per agent, an AI-BOM of the model estate, and a prioritized action queue. A second table scores the **OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications** (ASI01-ASI10, published December 2025) beside the LLM one, because they answer different questions: the LLM list governs what a model says, the agentic list governs what a system does, and an orchestrator with fallback chains, swarm fan-out, tool access and cross-run memory is squarely the second. Same discipline, every status read from observable state: goal hijack is partial because every point where one model's output becomes another's prompt is fenced as data with a content-derived nonce, while the answer an orchestrator reads back carries only a convention and a credential warning, tool misuse tracks the policy default (gap with no rules, partial over default-allow, configured over default-deny), identity and privilege abuse is enforced by the per-provider credential allowlist, cascading failures needs a graph.json and reports gap without one, and rogue agents falls to gap the moment the ledger chain breaks, since the record that would show an agent acting outside policy is the thing that just became untrustworthy. `hyctl security trifecta` is the audit the CSA recommends before releasing an agent: which dispatches carried **private data**, **untrusted content** and **external communication** at once, since any one capability is fine and all three together is what turns a poisoned input into exfiltration with no software vulnerability involved. Counted per dispatch from the provenance the egress gate records, and the headline is *exposure*, not presence: a trifecta the gate refused is reported as contained, because a dashboard that flags a working control trains people to ignore its own number. A dispatch with no recorded provenance is not counted at all rather than rendered as zero, so events predating the gate cannot read as a clean bill of health. `--exec` prints the executive summary; `--attest` emits a checkable attestation (posture + evidence state + rules in force + digest) that says plainly when the underlying log is not tamper-evident. `--json` and `--csv` for machine-readable output. Every ledger-derived string is stripped of control characters before it reaches a terminal, so a hostile tool name cannot rewrite the line it is printed on. The default view states in words what no number on it can, and derives it from the models actually discovered rather than asserting it: a model Hydra reaches over HTTP is **governed**, because Hydra composes that request and the gate sees every byte, while a model with an executable is a separate program Hydra hands the work to, running in a process it does not control, so the figures describe what Hydra sends and records and not what such a model independently reads and ships. The opaque models are named, not counted, and the test is the executable rather than a list of vendor names, so a local model served on :11434 reads as governed while the `ollama` binary on PATH does not. A subprocess model declared local-only runs behind a network gate: Hydra routes it through a local proxy that refuses every destination except loopback, private and link-local IP literals and `localhost`, and never sends a refused name to DNS. A model that ignores its proxy environment and opens a raw socket is still unseen, so the gate narrows the boundary without closing it. Those served models are checked rather than assumed: `hyctl security` asks each local model server what version it is and whether it answers on an address other than loopback, since Ollama ships with no authentication and prints no warning when bound to `0.0.0.0`, and a server reachable from the network is the one thing that falsifies the local-first claim outright. The probe compares the same identity endpoint discovery already uses, between loopback and this machine's own addresses, so nothing leaves the machine and an unrelated listener on the same port is not mistaken for the model server. A host firewall that drops the probe looks exactly like a server that is not listening, so a loopback-only result is reported as the weaker evidence it is. `--advisories` additionally asks OSV what is published against the versions it read, off by default because it is the only part of the report that leaves the machine. Advisories with a fix are separated from advisories without one, since upgrading answers the first and cannot answer the second: a current Ollama carries nine with no fix upstream, so one total would read identically on a patched server and an abandoned one. Hydra's own state directory is read the same way: a directory group or others can **write** is one in which the agent-binary baseline and the ledger's chain anchor can be replaced, so both would then report what the writer chose, and that is the finding; merely readable is reported separately, since it leaks the listing rather than the contents. It is read from the mode alone, so an ACL or a foreign-owned directory is outside what it saw, and Windows reports not evaluated rather than a pass. Nothing is repaired: the report is a read. and the guarantee reads as total only on a machine where nothing opaque can be routed to at all. The LLM list scored is the **2026** edition (OWASP-GenAI-LLM-Top-10-2026-v1.0, published 4 August 2026), where seven of the ten entries moved: Excessive Agency rose from LLM06 to LLM03, Improper Output Handling fell from LLM05 to LLM10, and 2025's System Prompt Leakage was replaced by the broader LLM08 Hidden Context Exposure, which covers every non-user-facing instruction the application assembles rather than the system prompt alone. Hydra scores that one from both directions: the egress gate declares `--system` and the a2a handoff on the way in, and a response repeating either back is recorded as a finding naming the model, since the category is about the model disclosing the context rather than the transport carrying it. The check is verbatim over a 96-character window and reports rather than refuses, and the detail says so, so `partial` is not read as more than it is. The file content an edit prompt embeds is deliberately excluded: `hyctl edit` getting its own file back is the answer, and a control that fires on every successful edit teaches people to ignore it. Category IDs carry the OWASP edition they belong to, in `--json`, in `--csv` and on every persisted score entry, because only LLM01 and LLM02 keep their number between editions: gap age is never computed across two of them, so a reordering restarts the clock rather than re-dating a different category's history, and a tracker keyed on an id can tell which list it read. The TUI cockpit's Audit view (`hyctl tui`) and the desktop app surface the same report visually
- `hyctl ask`: the tasks Hydra parked waiting on a human decision (`list`, `answer`, `decline`). A ledger policy rule can answer `ask` rather than allow or deny; dispatch then stops **before invoking any executor** and stores the task under `logs/pending/<task-id>.json` so it survives the process. An `ask` is not a denial and does not fall through to the next model in the fallback chain, skipping the model that needs permission and running a cheaper one would mean the question is never asked. Approval is per model, so answering for one model never authorizes another. `decline` records a denial in the ledger and runs nothing; an empty answer is not an answer and leaves the task parked. The desktop app surfaces the same queue
- `hyctl oracle`: verification oracles as calibrated evidence: `verify` runs any command that judges an answer (a test suite, a schema check, a script of your own) and maps its exit code to a log-likelihood ratio; `ground` checks an answer against the context its prompt carried
- **Grounding**: `hyctl oracle ground --prompt <file> --candidate <file>` verifies that an answer's claims appear in the context the model was given. It answers one narrow question with high precision, does the answer state a number, date, name, path, flag or symbol, or quote a phrase, that appears nowhere in the prompt, which is extrinsic hallucination: a model contradicting ground truth sitting in its own context. Dates are compared in one form, so `3 March 2026`, `March 3` and `2026-03-03` match each other, a source that gives the year supports the date without it, and a relative date such as "last Tuesday" is not checked. A name is two or more capitalised words, at least one of them a word the text never writes in lowercase, so "Priya Raman" is a name and "Task Manager" is not; a surname on its own is not checked, and a full name the source gives only as a surname is flagged. It needs no model, so it works only for scripts with capital letters. A phrase of three or more words in straight or curly double quotes has to appear in the prompt word for word, ignoring case, spacing, an ellipsis and a closing full stop; single quotes are skipped, since apostrophes make them unpairable. Quotes are not checked when the fenced context looks like code (a markdown code fence, or one line in five ending in `{`, `}`, `;` or `)`), because comments in code quote made-up speech and terms; the numbers and symbols in the answer still are. Everything else it declines. A prompt with no fenced context produces no verdict at all, and neither does an answer that states nothing checkable, because "nothing to check" and "checked and fine" are different facts and only one is evidence. Measured on 253 of this repository's own files, 690 pairs: it flagged 396 of 397 answers that were not grounded in the context they were scored against, including **184 of 184** where a single identifier had been swapped, which is the confident-contradiction case. Sensitivity on the same set is 0.535 and is a lower bound, since the positives are doc comments, which legitimately name sibling packages and issue numbers their own file does not contain. The verdict reaches `internal/trust` through the same calibrated LLR path a test suite's does, and until that source has both a positive and a negative recorded against it the command reports **insufficient evidence** instead of a number: an unobserved source's LLR is the prior wearing a measurement's clothes. It never rewrites. Its exit code is the verdict, as `hyverify`'s is: 0 grounded, 1 unsupported, 2 not checked, so a script can gate on it and "not checked" never reads as a pass; `--span` attaches the verdict to the span that produced the answer so `hyctl trace view` shows it. `--by-sentence` checks one sentence at a time and prints each numbered, then `supported [report L12-14]` with the fenced block and lines that back it, `NOT SUPPORTED: number 1.9`, or `nothing to check`, with the same exit codes; it only reports. With `--json` it prints a stable shape for scripts: `{"v":1,"sentences":[{"n","text","status","unsupported":[{"text","kind"}],"sources":[{"label","start_line","end_line"}]}],"supported":N,"not_supported":N,"nothing_to_check":N}`, where status is `supported`, `not_supported` or `nothing_to_check`. `hyctl dispatch --check gen` prints the same block under a claims check
- `hyctl compare <head-a> <head-b> --kind <kind>[.<area>]`: two models side by side on one kind of work, from your own checked answers, with no model calls. Per model: checked answers, pass rate, its 95% Wilson lower bound, and the record since its last change if it had one. It names one model ahead only when its lower bound is above the other's upper bound, on the record since any change; otherwise it says there is no clear difference yet and about how many more checked answers each would need. Cost per checked answer prints as unknown until cost rows are joined to checked answers. `--json` for scripts
- `hyctl recipe list [--kind k]`: print each kind of work's menu of recipes (model, samples, checks, stop rule) from `registry/recipes.yaml`. Code, extraction and classification have menus; every other kind runs one call. A recipe whose check the request did not bring is skipped, and a `dispatch --kind` run log says why. Nothing picks among a menu yet.
- `hyctl workflow`: run a multi-step task where each step is routed on its own (`run --step/--enum/--needs/--writes/--context/--reads`, `list`, `show`, `resume`, `rm`). `run --step-check N=<check>` gives step N any `hyctl dispatch --check` and `--step-kind N=<kind>` its kind of work: a step whose check really fails reruns once on a model measured stronger at that kind, sent the rejected answer and the error, and a step still failing is marked failed so its output never reaches a step that needs it. Each workflow keeps one store of context blocks addressed by content hash, saved with its record: `--context tickets=tickets.csv` stores a file once, and only the steps whose `--reads` name `tickets` are given it. Every step's output is kept there as a block too. A block over 4 MiB is refused rather than cut. Triage can go to a free local model and the fix to a frontier one, rather than one routing level for the whole task, and each step records which model answered, at which routing level, for how much. A step can name the steps it needs with `--needs` (paired with `--step` by position, `--needs 1,2`, or `--needs ""` for none); without it a step needs every earlier one, as before. Steps whose needs are done run at the same time, at most four at once, so a support-ticket run can extract once and then summarise and draft replies side by side, each on its own model. `--writes` names what a step writes (a path, `doc:<name>#<section>`, `record:<table>/<id>`), and two steps that write the same thing never run together; a whole document clashes with each of its sections, and two code files linked in `graph.json` count as one. A step gets the output of the steps it needs, each fenced as untrusted data, so no step is writing the next one's instructions. A failed step stops new steps from starting; steps already running finish and are recorded, and the ones that needed it stay pending for `resume`. It carries a dispatch's own safety caps, once per step rather than once per run: `policy.yaml`'s `max_cost_usd` and `max_wall_seconds` are enforced through the same code `hyctl edit` and `hyctl parallel` use, so a refusal reads identically, and `--max-cost`, `--local` and `--dry-run` are on `run`, with `--dry-run` printing each step's routing chain and ceiling before any money moves. What a run was started under, its system prompt, `--local` and `--max-cost`, is stored on the record, so `resume` continues under the same instructions rather than none; a flag given to `resume` overrides one. State is written *before* every step runs, not after, so a process killed mid-step leaves a record saying which step was in flight; `resume` continues from there and never re-runs a step that already produced output, so resuming does not pay twice. `list` and `show` say **interrupted** rather than running once the process that was writing the record is gone, and name the resume command, because a status is only ever what the last writer knew: a killed run used to read as running for ever and nothing said it was waiting on you. A second runner over a live workflow is refused rather than started: the heartbeat is claimed exclusively, so two `resume`s in the same instant cannot both dispatch every remaining step, and `run --id` of an id already stored is refused instead of overwriting it. `show` is the audit view: each step's model, routing level and cost, and every completed step's output, not only the last. A finished step reads "done, checked" only when it had a check and every check ran on its answer; one with no check, or whose check could not run, reads "done, not checked", and a line under the table counts them ("1 of 3 done steps checked"), so a run whose every step says done is not mistaken for a verified one. `show --json` carries the same as a `checked` bool per step (false on records from before it existed); `show --json` is the same record `show` prints each step's cost and every completed step's output, not only the last answer.
- `hyverify --version` reports the build, because this is the one binary shipped to repos with no `hyctl` beside it to ask, and the corpus it writes is kept verbatim and forever, so "which build wrote this row" gets asked later. `hyverify` is a second binary, the standalone verifier: it runs the command that judges a repository against a candidate file and records the verdict as a labelled example, with no router, no model selection and no Hydra config, so a corpus can be filled without adopting Hydra. It resolves what judges the work through the same code `hyctl edit` uses, never a second copy, or the two could disagree about whether work passed; nothing configured to judge the work is reported rather than treated as a pass; and it refuses a candidate that is neither named in the verifier's command nor inside the directory that command runs in, because a verdict is evidence about an answer only if the answer reached the thing the oracle inspects. Its exit code is the verdict: 0 verified and passed, 1 verified and failed, 2 no verdict at all. `--embed-model` vectorises the task through the same normalisation `hyctl edit` uses, so the example counts toward what a prompt classifier can be fitted on; without it the record is still real ground truth but `internal/classify` skips it, which is how the standalone verifier first shipped filling a corpus it could not read. It is off unless named, because the tool's contract is that it needs no services. The corpus directory it creates ignores itself, so a repository it verifies does not end up committing a second copy of its own source.
- **Redact, send, restore**: `hyctl dispatch --redact` replaces every detected value with a numbered placeholder (`<<EMAIL_1>>`, `<<CREDIT_CARD_1>>`) before a hosted model sees the request, then puts the real values back into the answer on your machine. A local model gets the original text. The map from placeholder to value stays in memory and is never sent or written. The same value gets the same placeholder across fallbacks and reruns, and the answer is restored before any check reads it. When the hosted answer needed a real value (it names a placeholder Hydra never issued, or says it cannot see one), the whole request reruns on a local model with the original text; with no local model, the hosted answer comes back with a note naming the placeholder. Measured in CI on a made-up corpus of support, HR, finance, log and legal texts (35 planted values): 0 detected values reached the hosted model, and every planted email, phone number, IBAN, card, SSN, IP address, AWS key id and credential was replaced; names and street addresses were not (0 of 7), since no pattern covers them. Re-run with `go test ./internal/dispatch -run TestRedaction_NoDetectedValueReachesRemote -v`. `--redact=names` (or `action = "redact-names"`) also has a local model that `hyctl policy ner` measured eligible on this machine list the names and street addresses, each sent as `<<PERSONAL_1>>`; with no eligible local model the pass is skipped and `hyctl egress receipt` says so, and a pass that fails or runs past two minutes sends nothing. `[policies.pii] action = "redact"` turns it on for every prompt with PII. A file the egress gate calls secret still goes only to a local model, or is refused. It runs on a single dispatch, not with `--swarm` or a confidence run, and the answer prints once restored rather than streaming.
- **PII and secret detection is a pattern list.** It drives local-only routing and redacts the opt-in payload, cache, embedding and retrieval stores before they are written. Besides formatted identifiers it catches `key = value` secrets in JSON and env files (`"api_key": "…"`, `OPENAI_API_KEY=…`), vendor keys (AWS, GitHub classic and fine-grained, GitLab, Slack tokens and webhooks, Stripe, npm, Hugging Face, Groq, OpenAI, Google), a bare 40-character AWS secret key, JWTs and authorization headers. It does not catch names, street addresses, a password with no name next to it, a secret split across lines or encoded, or a vendor format not in the list.
- `hyctl policy ner`: measures a model at the half of PII detection no pattern reaches. The regex detectors cover formatted identifiers; names, street addresses and organisations have no format, and on the presidio-research set they are 1,509 spans no pattern can reach. A model can read them and only some models can, so this asks one model 100 labelled texts and reports recall and false-positive rate **separately**, because each alone is trivially passed: answering NO to everything scores a flawless false-positive rate and answering YES to everything scores perfect recall. Measured locally over 470 labelled texts, a 7B scored 0.87 recall at 0.00 false positives while a 0.5B scored 0.86 recall and said yes to 94% of the negatives, clearing a recall bar by answering yes to nearly everything, which is why one number cannot decide this. Both halves are judged on the 95% Wilson interval rather than the point estimate, so a model is eligible only when the sample is large enough to say so: on 40 positives the half-width was 0.124, wider than the gap between two runs of the same model. Decoding is pinned greedy through `executor.Request.Temperature`, a pointer because 0 is the meaningful value and cannot spell provider-default the way MaxTokens does; without it the same model scored 0.82 and 0.72 on consecutive runs and the verdict flipped with it. A thinking model that spends its whole output budget before answering is reported as unreadable rather than as a no: a detector that reports clean because the model malfunctioned is worse than no detector. It defaults to a local model, since the command whose subject is privacy must not quietly pick one that leaves the machine. The report is saved per model, and only a local model that passed on this machine is asked by `hyctl dispatch --redact=names`.
- `hyctl eval`: the corpus of oracle-verified examples. `list` takes `--failed`, `--limit`, `--json`; `stats` reports pass rate by task type; `readiness` reports, per routing enum, whether the corpus can yet support fitting a routing choice from it; `training` answers the different question of whether a prompt classifier could be fitted, reporting vectors per embedding model and never summing across them, since two models put one sentence in different spaces and a total over both describes a corpus that does not exist. `classify` goes one step further and asks whether the vectors are worth anything: leave-one-out over the corpus, predicting for each held-out example the pass rate of the enum it actually used, scored as Brier with the Murphy decomposition. Resolution is compared against a permutation null, the best any of 19 outcome shuffles reaches over the same neighbourhoods, because a finite corpus produces resolution from chance alone and reporting that as a finding is how a router gets fitted on noise. Nothing routes on it: a measured classifier has to earn that separately. An oracle verdict on a real candidate is ground truth, so unlike traces these are kept verbatim and never pruned, they live at `~/.hydra/evalset/`, deliberately outside `logs/` so nothing that prunes logs can reach them. Deduplicated on (task, candidate), where the task is the prompt when the writer knows it and falls back to task type and source when nobody named it, and PII is marked rather than dropped, since dropping it would bias the corpus. The corpus is your own code and prompts and never leaves the machine: there is no upload path, no Hydra package that can reach the corpus imports anything that opens a socket or execs, and the third-party packages it rests on are pinned by name, all enforced by a test rather than stated as an intention. Sharing one would need an explicit opt-in and a separate redacted corpus, not this file
- Each example records the routing decision it judges (enum, routing level, model), so the corpus can be grouped by the thing `routing.yaml` is keyed on. `hyctl oracle verify` takes `--enum`/`--tier`, and reads both off the span when `--span` names one. Five things fill the corpus: `hyctl edit`, the edit tasks in `hyctl parallel`, `hyctl oracle verify --candidate`, `hyverify`, and `hyctl dispatch --check`. A checked dispatch files one example per answer under its kind of work, so `hyctl dispatch --kind summary --check ground` adds a row under `summary.general`, and trains the model that answered there; an answer that was not checked files nothing. An edit writes the change to disk and then runs the language validator against that file, so the pass or fail is about the content the model actually produced, and a rejected edit is recorded too before it is rolled back. An edit with no validator configured for the extension records nothing, because nothing judged it, and `validator_passed` comes back null rather than true for the same reason: "not checked" and "checked and passed" were reported identically before, and the first was most of them, Go included, since the shipped registry had no Go validator at all until it was given one. `hyctl dispatch --verify` is refused outright (`--check` is the dispatch check that reads the answer itself): a dispatch applies nothing to disk, so its verifier judges the working tree rather than the answer, and recording that as ground truth would label the corpus, and the calibration, with an unrelated outcome. The readiness floor is per (enum, model) pair, 25 examples on each of 2 models: measured on RouterEval and CodeRouterBench, a table fitted below roughly 10 observations per class loses to simply using the strongest model, and 25 is the first count whose gain interval excludes zero. Volume on a single model is not evidence about a different one, so it never counts toward readiness. Each example also carries the embedding of the instruction and the model that produced it, when an embedding model is on the machine: the task key is a hash, which is designed so that two similar prompts land nowhere near each other, and measuring a routing key rather than taking the caller's word for it needs the opposite. Both fields are stored or neither, because a vector without its model cannot be compared to anything. New examples also keep the task text, the instruction rather than the prompt the model saw, so a verified answer can later be shown with its question. It is kept like the answer: PII in either marks the example, and `hyctl eval list --json` never prints the task of a PII example
- **Run traces**: every dispatch writes a span, not just a cost row. A span carries its own identity and parent, severity, input and output tokens (with the cache reads and writes inside the input, where the provider reports them), time to first token where the provider reports it, and an open metadata map for model parameters, so a run answers what was asked, what came back, and how the fallback chain moved, rather than only what it cost.
