Span ids are OTLP span ids, so `hyctl trace export` carries the same identity **and the same parent** a collector sees, and a run arrives there as the tree `hyctl trace view` shows rather than as a flat list; each cost row names the span that spent the money, and the export joins the two. Each dispatch that ranks its heads also writes one route event on the task's span: every candidate in the order tried, with its measured score, how many results that score rests on, its nominal cost and whether it passed or which check dropped it, plus the runner-up and the chance the first pick was chosen. The export carries it as `hydra.route.*`. The task's span also names the recipe it ran: which model, how many answers to sample, which checks judge them, when to stop and what runs next. Every request today runs the one-call recipe, which stops on its checks when it has any. Structure is cheap by construction: a fully detailed span is 41 bytes on disk once sealed, because anything derivable from another field on the line (an info level, a parent that is just the task's span) is left off the wire and recomputed on read
- `hyctl trace view [run-id]`: a run as a waterfall of nested spans. One row per span with its position and extent drawn on the run's timeline, so a fallback chain reads as sequential and a swarm reads as overlapping, with model, routing level, status, tokens both ways, cost and time to first token beside it. No argument means the newest run. Spans that have been judged show their verdict in a column of its own, separate from whether the call succeeded. An answer a check rejected is scored `check=0` with the reason, and the attempt that replaced it reads `escalated from <span>`, so an escalation shows as one decision. `--span <id>` drills into one span and shows its verdicts and the prompt and response behind it, with the system prompt kept apart from the task; when that text is not there it says which of "capture is off", "not stored" and "evicted" applies rather than rendering an empty box. `--json` gives the whole nested structure. Runs recorded before spans existed still render: their events are grouped by the model they name
- `hyctl trace score [run-id] --span <id> --name <n> --value <v>`: a verdict on a span, so a trace answers whether the answer was right beside what it cost. Appended after the fact rather than written into the span, because a test suite finishes long after the dispatch it judges and a judgement must never rewrite what the model itself reported. Above zero passes, and any failing score fails the span, so one passing check cannot hide a failing one; a span nobody judged renders as unjudged, never as passed. A score naming a span the run does not contain is refused rather than silently orphaned. `hyctl oracle verify --span <id>` attributes its own verdict the same way, which is what closes the loop: the oracle already computes a calibrated LLR and previously had nowhere to put it
- `hyctl trace`: trace storage and analysis (`seal` (`--older-than`, `--dry-run`, `--json`), `payloads` (`--json`), `embeddings` (`--json`), `cache` (`--json`), `search` (`--limit`, `--json`), `evaluate` (`--policy`, `--confidence`, `--clip`, `--days`, `--json`), `export` (`--otlp`, `--out`, `--limit`, `--days`). `seal` folds run logs older than a cutoff into one compressed segment per month. This is lossless relocation, not retention: every event still reads back through the same commands and the desktop app afterwards. What it recovers is disk, one file per run is charged a whole filesystem block, so 65 short runs holding 27 KB of events were measured occupying 240 KB. `payloads` reports the **opt-in** store of prompt and response text, which is what a span's input and output refs point at: off unless chosen at `hyctl init`, and anything matching a secret detector is replaced before it is written, redaction happens before hashing, so the content address does not leak a fingerprint of the secret. Content is chunked before it is hashed, split at the prompt's natural segments and then at content-defined boundaries, so a system prompt repeated across every dispatch is stored once and a file re-read after an edit costs one chunk rather than a whole new copy: measured 10.3x against 2.6x for whole-prompt hashing on the first case and 8.8x against 3.0x on the second. Blobs are packed rather than stored one file each, measured 22.2x smaller on disk for 200 small blobs (allocated space, not logical bytes), and compressed with a dictionary trained from your own corpus. The store is bounded by a **byte budget rather than by sampling**, dropping whole oldest packs past it, so every run you have is readable in full instead of one run in ten; a ref whose pack has been dropped reads as missing rather than as the half that survived. A payload can be pinned, and a pack holding a pinned payload or one of its chunks is never dropped, even when that leaves the store over budget; `payloads` reports the pinned bytes. `embeddings` reports the **opt-in** store of one vector per dispatch, produced by an embedding model already running on this machine under Ollama: nothing is sent anywhere, text is redacted before it is embedded, and the model and its dimension are part of the store's key, so changing the model invalidates the store rather than silently comparing two vector spaces. It reports the three states apart, capture off, capture on with no model installed, and ready, because the middle one is otherwise silent. A 768-dimension vector costs 3,096 bytes, so the default 64 MB budget holds about 21,600 dispatches, and the oldest are dropped past it. `search` finds past dispatches whose prompt resembles a query, by two scorers over the same documents fused by rank: a lexical BM25 index that needs no model at all, and cosine over the stored vectors when an embedding model is installed. The lexical half is the point, because this corpus is code and the discriminating tokens are identifiers and flags, which is exactly where embeddings are weakest. Measured on 400 real commit subjects from this repository, known-item retrieval scores 99.7% precision at 1 lexically against 96.5% densely, where random would be 0.25%; and on prompts differing by a single identifier, `--max-cost` against `--max-heads` and `internal/awsconf` against `internal/executor` sit at 0.86 cosine, above the 0.85 a dense-only cache would treat as a hit, while the lexical index separates them by about 40%. Fusion is reciprocal rank rather than a weighted sum, because a BM25 score and a cosine are not on a common scale; with no embedder the fused result is the lexical result exactly, so there is no second code path to keep correct. A bag of words costs about 128 bytes against a vector's 3,096. `cache` reports the **opt-in** answer cache: how many answers it holds, how many dispatches it served against how many it was asked about, how much spend that avoided at what those answers cost to produce, and how many prompts the content gate refused after the similarity alone would have served them, which is the number that says whether the gate earns its place. `evaluate` answers what a routing policy you did **not** run would have cost, from the dispatches you did, self-normalized inverse propensity scoring with a percentile bootstrap interval, never a bare point estimate. Where the router had no chance of doing what the candidate policy would do it **refuses** rather than answering: that question is unidentifiable, not merely uncertain, and a wide interval still reads as a number. It reports effective sample size and whether weights were clipped, and distinguishes a log written before propensity logging existed from one with no overlap, because only the second is fixable by raising `explore_rate`. `--policy constraint` evaluates the cheapest-measured-competent router, which needs the task type each dispatch ranked on: rows carry that from now on and older ones cannot be evaluated at all, which it reports as its own count rather than folding into the same refusal. It also asks the machine what that policy would choose *today*, so an estimate over old contexts is read against current calibration, not the calibration of the time. `export` renders runs as OpenTelemetry spans over OTLP/HTTP, read from the run log so nesting, severity, time to first token and the open metadata map survive the trip, with spend joined on from the cost log by span id and cache reads and writes as `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens`; a dispatch logged before span ids existed still exports, as a root, since dropping it would lose spend a collector used to see. Nothing leaves the machine unless `--otlp` names an endpoint, and `HYDRA_OTLP_HEADERS` (`"k=v,k=v"`, the same shape `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` uses) carries auth, which every hosted collector needs and a local one on `:4318` does not; a malformed pair is refused rather than dropped, since silently sending an unauthenticated request turns your own typo into the collector's 401. and Hydra's own fields (routing level, enum, cost, propensity) are carried under `hydra.*` rather than dropped into a `gen_ai.*` shape that has no place for them)
- `hyctl models`: model capability scores (`list`, `add`, `remove`, `sync`, `pull`). This is a catalogue of scores, not an inventory of what is installed, so `list` marks which entries this machine can actually route to right now and counts them ("3 of 29"), from the same `health.Reason` that `probe`, `status` and the router use. An API provider with no key set, or a CLI agent that is not installed, reads as not routable rather than as available. `add` records a score for a model a provider must still discover and says what would make it routable (an API key, a local server, a registry entry); it does not create a routable entry. A locally served model is scored under the id `hyctl probe` prints (`ollama/qwen3:8b`), not the bare model name, and `add` says so rather than letting an entry no model reads look like it worked. `pull` is the one that does: it fetches a model into the local Ollama server and names the model the router will then use, read back from the server rather than derived from what you typed. The ref is whatever that server resolves, an Ollama library name or a HuggingFace GGUF repo (`hf.co/<user>/<repo>`), so HuggingFace is a ref shape rather than a separate mode. A model larger than this machine's usable memory is refused from the size the server reports on the first chunk, seconds in rather than an hour later when it would fail to load, and `--force` overrides for a machine with more headroom than it reports. This is the only command in hyctl that downloads weights, and nothing does it as a side effect of anything else
- `hyctl parallel`: fan N independent tasks out to N models at once, from a task JSON file. An edit task whose validator fails reruns once on a model measured stronger, the same rerun as `hyctl edit`, and its result reports `escalated` and `first_head`; text tasks have no check and never rerun.
- `hyctl edit`: scoped, validated, rollback-safe single-file edit. When the validator fails the file, the edit reruns once on a model measured stronger at that kind of file, sent the failed answer and the validator's output, within what is left of `max_cost_usd`; its JSON output reports `escalated` and `first_head`. A reply that is exactly one fenced block is taken as the file, and an unknown `--enum` is refused before any model runs.
- `hyctl review`: code review
- `hyctl vet`: review a diff and report what is wrong with it (`--from`/`--to`, `--commit`, `--json`, `--dry-run`, `--local`, `--enum`/`--tier`, `--exclude`, `--concurrency`). With no flags it reads the workspace: staged, unstaged and untracked together. File selection and the review rules come from open-code-review's delegate mode, which resolves both with no model, no API key and no spend; Hydra routes each file to a model of its own, so cost, policy, fallback and per-task-type calibration apply the way they do to any dispatch, and the model measured best at reviewing Go on this machine is the one asked about a `.go` file. One dispatch per file rather than per rule group, because a group can span a whole language and one prompt holding every Go file in a branch both blows the context and makes a reported line number unattributable. Findings are graded blocking or non-blocking, the two words the rule packs themselves use, and a model that did not say blocking has not claimed it blocks. Four things it refuses to guess at: a reply it cannot read as findings is retried once with a stricter instruction, since a CLI agent given a single-shot review often narrates the tool step it would take next rather than answering, and only a reply that fails twice is reported as unreadable rather than as a clean file (one dispatch per file only: a `--confidence` ensemble is not re-asked, since that would sample every model again); a finding naming a file the model was never shown is discarded and counted; a file no rule matched is not reviewed at all; and a delegate schema it was not written against is refused on both of its calls, the file preview and the rule document, since a silent mis-parse reads as "no findings" and that is the one wrong answer a reviewer must never give. The commit message is passed as review background, fenced and labelled as a claim rather than an instruction, because in a review its author is the party under scrutiny. `--confidence <float>` reviews each file with as many Models as its blast radius warrants instead of one: `internal/graph` gives the file's transitive dependents, `internal/trust`'s defect model turns that into a confidence-of-correctness target, and the SPRT ensemble samples Models in most-diagnostic-per-dollar order and stops the moment the target is reached, so a leaf file costs one cheap Model and a hub-core file gets as many as it takes. The value is a floor and the blast radius only ever raises it. Three things it will not fudge: a radius Hydra did not read off a graph is reported as a default rather than a measurement, a file that never reached its target is marked so its findings stand while its confidence does not, and a task type where no Model has measured accuracy yet stops **that task type** once with the command to record an outcome rather than paying the same refusal for every file, since calibration is keyed per task type and a Go refusal says nothing about the JavaScript files the ensemble could have reviewed. Every file in scope is listed with an outcome whichever way the run stopped, so the "n/m reviewed" denominator is the real one. Every ensembled file's run is **recorded** with the log-odds ledger of who voted, and the report names the `hyctl trust outcome <task_hash>` command that replays it once you know whether a finding was real. That trains the dissenters too, which is the only observation that can move a Model's specificity, and it is why a review is a better training signal than `hyctl trust record`, which can only say a source was right about its own answer. Nothing is trained automatically from the ensemble's own answer, because a run asserting it was correct is circular. `--confidence 0`, the default, keeps one dispatch per file and records nothing, and `--max-cost` refuses a Model whose estimated cost for a file exceeds it, on the single-dispatch path as well as the ensemble one. `--local` binds the ensemble's equivalence judge as well as the Models it samples: that judge carries the whole prompt and both answers, so a local-only review keeps them on the machine and falls back to comparing the text when no local Model can judge. Exits 3 on a blocking finding and 4 when no file was reviewed at all, in both the table and `--json`: reviewing nothing is not a pass, and exiting 0 on it made `hyctl vet || exit 1` read a totally failed review as clean. With `--confidence` the banner that says whether the blast radii are measurements goes to stderr, so stdout under `--json` is one document a parser can read. open-code-review is a separate install (`npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`) and its absence is reported as exactly that, with the install line, rather than as a decode error With `--confidence`, agreement is counted per finding rather than per file: the ensemble already produces every Model's answer, so a claim three of four Models made renders as 3/4 and one only one of them made as 1/4, where before both carried the file's single confidence and looked identical. Findings are matched on file, line and severity, and the report says so, because the same defect a line away or worded differently counts as its own claim and the count is a lower bound rather than a measurement of how many Models really agreed.
- `hyctl serve`: expose the router as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`--addr`, `--token`, `--enum`, `--local`), serving `POST /v1/chat/completions` and `GET /v1/models`. Any tool that speaks OpenAI then routes through Hydra, so policy, fallback, per-task-type calibration and spend logging apply the way they do to `hyctl dispatch`, and the spend shows up in `hyctl cost` like any other call. The `model` field is the routing instruction, which makes a client's model picker into Hydra's routing UI: `hydra` takes the default enum (`--enum`, `STANDARD` unless set). Routing by objective is opt-in, with `--objective` or the `X-Hydra-Objective` header per request: `quality` tries the head measured strongest in the task class first, and `cost` the cheapest one measured competent; under quota pressure it falls back to `STANDARD`, and the answer echoes `X-Hydra-Objective` and `X-Hydra-P-Pass-Basis`. `quality` becomes the default in v2.0.0: until then a `hydra` request naming no objective, on a server started with neither `--enum` nor `--objective`, gets a `Deprecation` header (RFC 9745) with a `Link` to the docs and one stderr warning per server start (`HYDRA_NO_DEPRECATION_WARNINGS=1` silences it); `hydra/standard` or an explicit `--enum STANDARD` keeps today's route after the change. `hydra/hard` or `hydra/t4` pin an enum or a routing level, and a model id pins that model. What comes back in a response's `model`, and on every stream chunk, is the answering model's **id**, so a client can send it straight back: SDKs echo that value into the next turn and group their logs by it, and the display name it used to carry was not something `/v1/models` advertises. The listing offers only models the router would actually run, so an embedding-only model is not in the picker at all rather than in it and refused. A model the client named that does not exist is **404**, one that cannot be used here, an embedding-only model or a cloud model on a `--local` server, is **400**, and 5xx is kept for a model that really failed: 5xx is in the OpenAI SDKs' default retry class, so grading a client's own mistake that way made it retry something that could never succeed and then report Hydra as broken. Tool calling is passed through on every chat dialect Hydra speaks: OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock and Cohere, each of which shapes tools differently and is translated rather than passed along. A model that writes its call as ordinary message text instead of in the structured field has that call **recovered**, so an agent loop continues instead of receiving a JSON blob it cannot act on: measured here, Ollama reports tool support for every local model while Qwen2.5-Coder:7b returns `{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {...}}` as the content every time and qwen3:0.6b, on the same install, returns a structured call. The recovery is deliberately narrow, because the alternative is inventing a reading: the whole trimmed content must be the call, the name must be one the caller actually offered, every element must parse or none are taken, and it runs only where the server reported no call at all, so a server that structures its own is never second-guessed. What it cannot do is tell a call from a model quoting one, because asked to show an example without calling, the model answers with exactly the bytes it sends to make the call: that ambiguity is the model's and is recorded as a known limit rather than papered over. The startup banner counts the models this endpoint can actually reach, and says they **accept tool definitions**, which is a property of the dialect rather than a promise about what the model will emit. Replicate is the exception, since its prediction API polls rather than chats and has no tool surface at all, and a model that cannot carry tool definitions is skipped rather than sent a stripped request, because a dropped tool array is not a degraded answer but a loop that never terminates. The startup banner says how many of the discovered Models can carry tools. It binds `127.0.0.1` and **refuses** an off-loopback bind that has no token rather than warning about it: this endpoint spends money and reads your code, and `hyctl security` reports exactly that risk about other local model servers. `stream: true` is answered as server-sent events, with usage on the final chunk when `stream_options.include_usage` asks for it and tool calls carried as `delta.tool_calls` fragments. A fallback before any output is invisible to the client; one after it ends the stream with an error naming the model, because SSE cannot take a partial back and appending the next model's answer to it would compose a reply no model ever gave. Every request is **one run**, and the identifier it is traceable by comes back in the `X-Request-Id` header and as the response's own `id`, one value in both places, set before anything is written so an error response carries it too and so the streamed path has it before the first chunk. `hyctl trace view <id>` resolves it. A server used to give every request one shared run, so a long-lived endpoint had a single ever-growing run and `hyctl trace view` with no argument showed the session rather than the last request, while the response's `id` was an unrelated random recorded nowhere: a client that got a bad answer could not find the trace for it. The run also records what the request was for, so a reader no longer falls back to the routing enum and renders a real question as "MODERATE" A client can name a dotted task class in the `X-Hydra-Task-Class` header (or the server sets one with `--task-class`): an unpinned request then routes on that class's calibration, skips the answer cache, forwards `temperature` (0 to 2; a model capped at 1 is skipped, and none left is a 400), and echoes the class in the header and a `hydra` body block. Without the header nothing changes. policy.yaml's `max_cost_usd` caps every request, and `X-Hydra-Max-Cost-USD` sets a per-request ceiling that can only lower it; a request the header refused outright is a 400. `X-Hydra-Redact: on` (or `[policies.pii] action = "redact"`) sends a hosted model placeholders for detected values and restores them in the reply and in tool-call arguments; `X-Hydra-Redacted` answers how many values were replaced. In a stream, a placeholder split across chunks is held back, never more than one placeholder long, until it can be restored. Each request is its own run, and the run records which chat it continues: a key hashed from the system message and the first user message, which a client resends unchanged every turn, or the `X-Hydra-Conversation` header (up to 128 bytes) for a client whose opening changes. Every request must name the bound address as its `Host` (any loopback name on a loopback bind), a request carrying an `Origin` header is refused unless `--allow-origin` lists it, and a POST must be `Content-Type: application/json`. Over `--max-inflight` (default 8) requests at once or `--rate` (default 120) a minute, a request gets 429 with `Retry-After`, which the OpenAI SDKs retry. A task class can carry verifiers, `[[serve.verifiers]]` in config.toml, each a `match` check against a labels file (one label per line, beside config.toml unless absolute) or a regular expression: a buffered, tool-free answer on an objective route is then checked, and while no verifier verdict makes it `--confidence` sure, the next model asked is one measured in that class to beat it, at most `--max-escalations` (default 2) times and within the request's or policy.yaml's cost ceiling. A verifier with no calibration in the class cannot escalate anything, and when every answer is rejected the most confident is served and never cached. A request can also name its own checks in `X-Hydra-Check`, one per header line: `ground` (the answer's figures and names must appear in the context the messages fenced), `match:pattern=<re>`, or `gen` (checks written for the `X-Hydra-Task-Class` kind by another model, run after the answer). Anything else is a 400 listing these. `ground` and `match` join the escalation the way a configured verifier does. The reply carries `X-Hydra-Check-Result` (`passed`, `failed` or `not_checked`) and a one-line `X-Hydra-Check-Detail`, and the same as `check_result` and `check_detail` under `hydra` in the body; a check that could not run is `not_checked`, never `passed`. Streamed and tool-calling requests are checked after the answer and never retried, and a stream carries the verdict in its final chunk's `hydra` field. It also serves `POST /v1/decisions` and `/v1/systemone` for decision models, which answer a fixed question with a probability per option instead of text: local sources are asked first, and a second source only when the first is not sure enough.
- `hyctl init`: first-run wizard: discover models and choose your main model
- `hyctl upgrade`: downloads the latest release archive, checks it against the release checksums (and its build provenance when `gh` is installed and signed in), installs nothing if a check cannot run, and renames the new binary over the old one, so the running process finishes on the old code and the next invocation picks up the new. Deliberately skipped for a Homebrew install, where overwriting brew's symlink would desync its bookkeeping, `brew upgrade hyctl` there instead
- `hyctl version`: build and version info

## How Hydra Differs From Other Routers

Cost routing and automatic fallback are table stakes. The rows that separate Hydra from
OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Portkey and vLLM Semantic Router are: local-first discovery (Hydra
finds the models already on your machine rather than taking a declared endpoint list),
verified answers (verifiers and a calibrated optimal-stopping SPRT ensemble decide
when an answer is good enough, not a single up-front classification), model ranking that learns from outcomes verified **on your machine**, an
on-device accountability ledger, and MCP server safety scoring. vLLM Semantic Router is the
closest on routing itself: it is self-hosted, its classifier runs locally so a routing
decision needs no network, and it routes per category rather than on one global "best"
model. What it does not do is calibrate from your own verified outcomes, keep an
append-only ledger of what was touched, or fetch the model.

## Who It's For

Anyone who sends work to AI models and wants each request answered by a model with a measured record on that kind of task, with the option to check the answer before relying on it: summarising documents, extracting fields, drafting replies, reviewing code. Developers reach it through the `hyctl` CLI or its OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`hyctl serve`), which any tool or coding assistant can point at; everyone else through the desktop app.

## Installation

The CLI binary is named `hyctl` (the product is Hydra). Available via:

```bash
brew trust ankit373/hydra && brew install ankit373/hydra/hyctl                    # Homebrew
npm install -g hyctl                                                              # npm
npx hyctl                                                                         # npx (no install)
pip install hyctl                                                                 # pip
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ankit373/hydra/main/install.sh | sh  # standalone (macOS/Linux)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ankit373/hydra/main/install.ps1 | iex        # standalone (Windows)
```

The desktop app installs separately, with its own script (macOS and Linux):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ankit373/hydra/main/install-app.sh | sh
```

It resolves the newest release tag (desktop asset names embed their version, so GitHub's `/latest/download/` shortcut cannot address them), verifies the download against the `.sha256` published beside it, installs the `.app` to `/Applications` on macOS or the binary to `~/.local/share/hydra` with a `~/.local/bin` symlink on Linux, and clears the macOS quarantine flag. `HYDRA_VERSION` pins a release; `HYDRA_APP_DIR` changes the install directory. Windows has no script, download `hydra-desktop_<version>_windows_amd64.zip` (or `_windows_arm64.zip`) from the releases page and unzip it.

Platform support: `hyctl` is built for macOS, Linux and Windows on both x86-64 and ARM64, six targets, every release. Homebrew covers macOS and Linux; npm/npx and pip cover all three OSes; `install.sh` covers macOS and Linux and `install.ps1` covers Windows (per-user, no admin rights; both verify the release checksum and refuse to install when it cannot be checked, unless `HYDRA_INSECURE=1`). The desktop app ships five targets every release: macOS (universal), Windows x86-64, Windows ARM64, Linux x86-64 and Linux ARM64. `install-app.sh` picks the right one automatically.

Or build from source (requires Go 1.26+):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ankit373/hydra && cd hydra && go build ./cmd/hydra
```

## Pricing

**Free and open source, MIT License.** No subscription. Bring your own API keys.

You pay the underlying model providers directly, at their own rates; local models via Ollama or llama.cpp cost $0. Hydra publishes no savings percentage: what it costs depends on your models and your work, and `hyctl stats` and `hyctl cost` report your own spend. Run `hyctl pricing list` for live rates, including cache read and write rates where the model lists them.
